lines.text: Why did one pair of hearing aids average $4,700?
lines.say: Why did one pair of hearing aids average forty-seven hundred dollars?

lines.text: That $4,700 was the 2013 average, per the National Academies.
lines.say: That forty-seven hundred was the 2013 average, per the National Academies.

lines.text: Reason one: it's bundled. The hearing test, fitting, follow-ups and adjustments are baked in.
lines.say: Reason one: it's bundled. The hearing test, fitting, follow-ups and adjustments are baked in.

lines.text: Reason two: five makers control about 90% worldwide, 84% in the US, per a 2026 estimate.
lines.say: Reason two: five makers control about ninety percent worldwide, eighty-four percent in the US, per a 2026 estimate.

lines.text: Reason three: Original Medicare generally doesn't pay for hearing aids, so people cover the bill.
lines.say: Reason three: Original Medicare generally doesn't pay for hearing aids, so people cover the bill.

lines.text: Since October 2022, an FDA rule lets adults with mild-to-moderate loss buy them over the counter.
lines.say: Since October 2022, an F D A rule lets adults with mild to moderate loss buy them over the counter.

lines.text: The White House put those pairs at $199 to $999.
lines.say: The White House put those pairs at one ninety-nine to nine ninety-nine dollars.

lines.text: Our math: $4,700 minus $999 leaves a $3,701 gap.
lines.say: Our math: forty-seven hundred minus nine ninety-nine leaves a thirty-seven hundred and one dollar gap.

lines.text: But OTC is only for mild-to-moderate loss, with no professional fitting.

post.ig:
Why did one pair of hearing aids average $4,700?
The 2013 average of $4,700 per pair bundled the test, fitting and follow-ups (National Academies).
Five makers control about 90% of the global market and 84% in the US (2026 estimate).
Original Medicare generally doesn't cover hearing aids. Since Oct 17, 2022, adults with mild-to-moderate loss can buy OTC pairs, launched at $199-$999.
Sources: National Academies (2016), Capitol Forum (2026), Medicare.gov, FDA, White House (2022).
